lines.text: Korean five A, chapter eight: modern Korean history. In this episode we go through all 109 words of chapter eight, in the order of the word list.
For every word you hear the Korean, what it means, a tip, and a short example. Say the Korean out loud with us.
Next section: the video lesson. This section covers the words from the video lesson about small habits that change your life, including food, willpower, and a few useful grammar patterns.
A noun meaning magic, a spell, or sorcery. It is used both for fairy tale magic and for something that feels magical.
The phrase to be put under a spell is a common way to say you are hooked on something.
저는 그 노래에 마법에 걸린 것 같아요.
I feel like I'm under a spell from that song.
An adverb meaning repeatedly or again and again. It often carries a slightly annoyed feeling about something you can't stop.
Use it before a verb, as in keep forgetting or keep thinking about something.
I keep making the same mistake.
A noun for a top quality item or an excellent piece. It is often used when praising food or a craft.
Restaurants like to use it to say a dish is the best of its kind.
The kimchi stew at this place is truly outstanding.
An adverb meaning mostly or mainly. It tells you what usually happens, not what always happens.
It is a handy word for describing your habits, like what you mostly eat or where you mostly go.
A verb meaning to live on your own, usually in a rented room while cooking for yourself. It is very common for students and young workers away from home.
It is not just living alone, it suggests looking after your own meals and chores.
I have lived on my own since university.
A noun for a daily meal, especially in the sense of getting enough to eat. It sounds a bit more serious than a simple word for a meal.
With the verb for solving, it means getting through a meal somehow, often cheaply or quickly.
I was busy, so I got through my meal at a convenience store.
An adverb meaning exactly, firmly, or sharply. It adds a feeling of decisiveness or a perfect fit.
With the verb for cutting off, it means quitting something completely, like a bad habit.
An adjective meaning to feel bloated or heavy in the stomach, especially after eating too much.
Koreans often use it when food sits badly, so you will hear it at the dinner table.
I overate, so my stomach feels bloated.
A noun meaning influence or effect. It is the standard word for how one thing affects another.
It pairs with the verb meaning to reach, so it literally means to reach an influence on something.
A noun meaning chain like or in a chain reaction. It describes things happening one after another, each causing the next.
Think of a chain reaction, like one small mistake leading to many more.
Problems came up one after another.
A noun meaning the most urgent task or top priority. It is a fairly formal word, common in news and meetings.
It combines the ideas of urgent and duty, so it is the thing you must do first.
Right now, protecting your health is the top priority.
A noun meaning will, determination, or resolve. It is about mental strength to do something.
Koreans often say a person with a strong will can do anything, so it shows up in motivation talk.
To succeed, you need strong willpower.
A noun meaning itself or in itself. It points to the thing alone, without anything around it.
Place it after a noun to say that the thing alone is the point, like the plan itself.
Just starting is difficult in itself.
An adverb meaning very, extremely, or tremendously. It is stronger than the plain word for very.
It is often used to emphasise something impressive, and it works in both speech and writing.
An adjective meaning grand or large in scale. It can sound slightly exaggerated, as if something is more elaborate than it needs to be.
People often use it in the negative to say a plan is not that big, just simple.
You don't need a grand plan.
A noun for a push up. The literal meaning is bending and stretching the arms, and the word is a familiar part of military and gym vocabulary.
It is counted with the usual counter for small items, so you can say ten push ups easily.
매일 팔 굽혀 펴기를 열 개씩 해요.
I do ten push ups every day.
An adverb meaning unconditionally or no matter what. It can also carry a stubborn feeling, as in absolutely must.
It often appears with a demand, so it can sound pushy if you are not careful.
We must finish by tomorrow, no matter what.
A verb meaning to put in, to bring in, or to invest. With the word for habit, it means to form a habit.
Remember the combo for building a habit, because it comes up in self improvement talk all the time.
I got into the habit of waking up early.
A noun meaning a sense of accomplishment. It is the good feeling you get after finishing something.
The set phrase uses the verb for tasting, so you literally taste a sense of achievement.
I tasted a sense of achievement after finishing my workout.
A noun that works like an adjective, meaning efficient or effective. It describes getting the most results with the least wasted effort.
It is a popular word in business and study advice, usually followed by the particle for describing something.
This method is the most efficient.
An adverb that means indeed, truly, or as expected. It shows that something lived up to what you had heard or imagined.
It is also used in questions to wonder whether something is really true.
As expected of a famous restaurant, it was delicious.
An adjective meaning easy or smooth, with no real difficulty. It describes tasks that go along without obstacles.
It sounds a bit more written and polite than the everyday word for easy.
This job was easier than I thought.
An adverb meaning quietly, subtly, or more than expected. It describes something that is not obvious on the surface.
It is great for mild surprise, as in it is quietly quite good, or he is secretly rather kind.
A grammar pattern meaning once you actually try something, you find that it is different from what you expected. It follows a verb.
Use it when your worry turned out to be unnecessary, or when reality surprised you.
Once I actually tried it, it wasn't hard.
A grammar pattern meaning only a small amount at most. It combines a word for just with a particle that needs a negative ending.
It expresses that the amount is smaller than expected, often with a disappointed or surprised feeling.
I only have five thousand won left.
Next section: reading one. This section covers the first reading, about modern Korean history: the division, the war, dictatorship, economic growth, and democratization.
A noun meaning highway or freeway. It is made of the words for high, speed, and road.
Korea's first major expressway, between Seoul and Busan, opened in 1970 and symbolised the push for economic growth.
A noun meaning communism. It is the political and economic system associated with North Korea's founders and the Soviet Union.
The ending that means ism appears in several political words, so learn it as a pattern.
A noun meaning the military or the army. It is a short, one syllable word that appears in many compounds.
You will often hear it in news about politics and defence.
The military is an organisation that defends the country.
A noun meaning the president of a country. It is the title for the head of state in South Korea.
Add the honorific ending after it when you talk about a specific president.
The president is elected every five years.
A noun meaning a dictator. It is made from the words for sole and rule, plus the suffix for a person.
Several of Korea's postwar presidents, such as Syngman Rhee, Park Chung hee, and Chun Doo hwan, were widely criticised as authoritarian.
That dictator ruled the country for a long time.
A noun meaning democratization, the process of becoming democratic. It is the key word of Korea's 1980s history.
The big milestone was 1987, when mass protests led to direct presidential elections.
A noun meaning division or separation, and in Korean history it refers to the split of the peninsula after 1945.
When Korea was liberated from Japan, the Soviet Union and the United States occupied the north and south, which led to two separate states.
한반도는 분단된 지 칠십 년이 넘었어요.
The Korean peninsula has been divided for over seventy years.
An expression meaning to receive criticism or to be criticised. It pairs the noun for criticism with the verb for receiving.
It is a formal, news style phrase, handy for talking about politicians and policies.
That policy received a lot of criticism.
A noun meaning casualties, or the people killed and wounded. It is common in reports about wars and disasters.
The Korean War caused millions of casualties, including many civilians.
Many casualties came out of the war.
A noun meaning the amount of exports, in terms of money. It is a typical word in economic news.
South Korea's exports passed ten billion dollars in 1977, a milestone of its rapid growth.
This year's export value rose sharply.
A noun meaning a demonstration or protest. It is often used in the phrase for joining a demonstration.
Student protests played a major role in Korea's democratic movement, especially in 1960, 1980, and 1987.
Students held a protest in the street.
A noun meaning a hero or heroine. It is used both for historical figures and for ordinary people who did something brave.
Admiral Yi Sun sin, who defeated the Japanese navy in the sixteenth century, is the most famous hero in Korean memory.
He was a hero of the people.
A noun meaning separated families, those torn apart by the division of the peninsula and the war.
Many were split in 1950, and those still alive are now very old, so the issue is urgent.
Separated families want to meet their relatives.
A noun meaning capitalism. Like communism, it is an ism word built on the same ending.
In the Cold War, South Korea sided with the capitalist West and North Korea with the communist bloc.
An expression meaning to carry out a military operation. It combines the noun for operation with the verb for starting something.
The verb for starting here suggests launching something big, not just doing it.
The army carried out a major operation.
A noun meaning hostility or antagonism, built from the words for enemy and feeling.
It describes deep bad feeling between groups, such as that left by the war.
A noun meaning command or leadership, especially in a military or team setting.
It often appears in the pattern under someone's command, so you will hear it in war stories.
They fought under the general's command.
A noun meaning evaluation or appraisal. It is a common word in school, work, and history writing.
Historians give a leader's legacy mixed evaluations, so this word fits Korean presidents well.
Opinions about that president are divided.
A verb meaning to attack or assault. It can be used for armies and also for criticising people.
North Korea attacked the South in June 1950, which started the Korean War.
A verb meaning to prohibit or ban. It is a formal word you see on signs and in laws.
It is stronger and more official than simply saying you cannot do something.
An expression meaning to exceed ten billion dollars. The verb for going beyond is attached to the amount.
This is the type of phrase used in economic news about records and milestones.
A verb meaning to stretch, grow, or increase. It describes a number or amount that gets bigger over time.
It works for things that grow naturally, like population, weight, or your Korean skills.
A verb meaning to crack down on or to enforce a rule. It is typical of police and government activity.
You hear it in news about traffic enforcement and illegal activities.
The police crack down on drunk driving.
A verb meaning to regain or take back something that was lost. It combines the idea of again with the verb for finding.
Seoul changed hands several times in the first year of the Korean War, so this verb fits that story.
An expression for a push and pull fight, a back and forth struggle where neither side wins clearly. It is a long phrase used for wars and games.
The Korean War had this character in 1951, with the front line moving back and forth across the peninsula.
The war was a back and forth struggle.
A verb meaning to start or to hold something, often something big like an event, a fight, or a debate.
It is less casual than the plain verb for doing, so use it for events and large activities.
A passive verb meaning to be selected or picked. It is the passive form of the verb meaning to pull out.
It is used for votes and contests, as in being elected or chosen.
He was chosen as class president.
A verb meaning to suppress or oppress. It describes using power to keep people down.
Authoritarian governments in Korea were accused of oppressing free speech.
The government suppressed the people's freedom.
A passive verb meaning to be occupied by force, used for land and cities taken by an army.
During the war, Seoul was captured by North Korean forces just three days after the invasion.
The capital was occupied by the enemy.
A verb meaning to restrict or limit. It is used for rules, access, and time.
It is a formal word, found in laws and notices.
A passive verb meaning to be destroyed. It is used for buildings, cities, and the environment.
After the war, almost all of Seoul's industry and infrastructure lay in ruins.
Many cities were destroyed by the war.
A verb meaning to be defeated or to lose. It is the formal verb for losing a battle or a match.
It is more serious than the everyday word for losing, so it suits war and sport reports.
Our team lost in the final.
A verb meaning to combine or unite things into one, including adding numbers together.
Use it for money, forces, or groups joining together.
They merged the two companies into one.
A phrase meaning numerous separated families, using the word for countless as a modifier.
It sets the scene for the big human cost of division, with millions of people affected.
A noun for the thirty eighth parallel, the line of latitude that divided the Korean peninsula in 1945.
It was drawn by American officers as a quick dividing line, and it became the base for the border between North and South.
The Korean peninsula was divided along the thirty eighth parallel.
A noun for a military coup, a takeover of government by the army. It uses a loan word for coup.
The best known coup in Korean history is the one led by Park Chung hee on the sixteenth of May, 1961.
The government changed through a military coup.
A noun for the Cold War, the long rivalry between the United States and the Soviet Union, without direct fighting between them.
Korea was one of its hottest fronts, because the peninsula was divided between the two blocs.
Korea was greatly affected by the Cold War.
A noun for a nighttime curfew, a ban on being out at night. It was strictly enforced in Korea for decades.
It was in place from 1945 and only abolished in 1982.
In the past, there was a nighttime curfew.
A noun for ceasefire talks, the negotiations to stop fighting. It uses the words for truce and meeting.
The talks dragged on for two years before an armistice was signed in July 1953.
The ceasefire talks continued for a long time.
Next section: reading two. This section covers the second reading, about the families split by the division and the emotional reunions that followed.
An adverb meaning by force or forcibly. It describes doing something against someone's will.
It is the key word in stories about people forcibly taken away during wars and occupation.
They were taken away by force.
A noun meaning an orphan, a child without parents.
The Korean War left many thousands of orphans, and some were adopted overseas.
Many orphans appeared because of the war.
A noun meaning pain or suffering. It can be physical or mental.
It is stronger and more general than the word for a simple ache, and it appears in serious writing.
A phrase meaning within South Korea. It uses the word for inside to show the scope.
You will see it in news and reports to limit a number to the South.
There are many separated families within South Korea.
A noun meaning a spouse or partner. It is a neutral, formal word for husband or wife.
It is the word you see on official forms, not in casual talk.
A noun that works like an adjective, meaning full scale or fully underway. It describes something that is truly getting started.
It is often followed by the verb for starting, as in something is really beginning now.
A noun for an editorial, the opinion piece of a newspaper.
It is a good word for reading practice, since editorials use lots of formal vocabulary.
A noun meaning a reunion of people who have been apart for a long time.
The first reunions of separated families between the two Koreas took place in 1985, and a larger series began in 2000.
A separated family reunion event was held.
A noun meaning a live broadcast. It combines the words for alive and broadcasting.
In 1983 a television program searching for separated families ran live for more than four months and moved the whole country.
A noun meaning a sea of tears, a place where everyone is crying together.
It is a vivid expression, made of the words for crying and sea.
The reunion hall became a sea of tears.
A noun for the Japanese colonial period, from 1910 to 1945.
It refers to the era when Japan ruled Korea, and it is a core topic in Korean modern history.
It was hard to use Korean writing during the Japanese occupation.
A phrase meaning seventeen times or on seventeen occasions. It uses the counter for repeated occasions.
The counter for occasions is useful for counting events, like meetings or visits.
The talks were held seventeen times.
A noun meaning dementia. It is the standard medical word.
In Korea, many elderly separated family members developed dementia before they could meet their relatives.
A noun for the escape route taken by refugees, or the journey itself while fleeing.
It is a word from the war years, when millions fled south on foot.
I was separated from my family on the road while fleeing.
A noun meaning a fleeting moment, a single instant.
It is used for how quickly things can change, like a life turning upside down in one moment.
Everything changed in a single moment.
A verb meaning to be taken or dragged away against your will. It is a passive form.
It is the right word for people forced away, such as conscripts and prisoners.
He was dragged off to the army.
A verb meaning to discuss, in a formal sense. It is used for meetings and negotiations.
It is more official than the everyday verb for talking, and you see it a lot in news.
An expression meaning to continue living apart from each other. It describes separation that lasts.
It captures the sadness of families living apart for decades.
The family lived apart for a long time.
A verb meaning to gather or crowd around. It describes a crowd of people rushing in.
It suggests a crowd arriving at once, not a small group.
A verb meaning to show or to put on a quality. With the word for leisure, it means to act in a relaxed, unhurried way.
In this expression it means taking your time, often a bit too much while others are in a hurry.
Now is not the time to take it easy.
A verb meaning to hurry or rush. It is usually used with a person as the subject who is speeding up.
You will often hear a parent say it to a child who is running late.
We have no time, so please hurry.
A verb meaning to pursue or seek. It is a formal verb used for goals, values, and ideals.
It is common in writing about what a society or person is aiming for.
A verb meaning to burst or make something pop. With the word for crying, it means to burst into tears.
It describes a sudden release, such as laughter, tears, or a balloon popping.
A verb meaning to spread. It is used for news, rumours, diseases, and feelings.
Feelings and information both spread this way, so it is very common in everyday speech.
An adverb meaning fortunately or luckily. It shows relief that things turned out fine.
Use it at the start of a sentence to share good news after a worry.
An adverb meaning completely or perfectly. It is used when something is totally the case.
It is common with both positive and negative statements, such as completely different or completely fixed.
An adverb meaning as it is or like this. It suggests leaving things in the present state.
It often appears in sentences like I can't go on like this, or let's leave it as it is.
I don't want to part like this.
An adverb meaning all at once or all at the same time.
It is useful when many things happen together, such as everyone speaking or many tasks arriving.
The people shouted all at once.
An expression meaning emotion spreading like ripples or waves. It is a poetic phrase used in writing.
It describes how a moving moment passes from one person to many.
The emotion spread like a wave.
An expression meaning to be unable to forget even in a dream. It means something is so deeply felt that it never leaves you.
It is used for longing, usually for family or hometown, as in the stories of separated families.
He could never forget his hometown, even in his dreams.
An expression meaning to pass away one by one. It uses a gentle phrase for leaving the world.
The phrase for leaving the world is a polite way to say someone has died.
이산가족들이 하나 둘 세상을 떠나고 있어요.
Separated family members are passing away one by one.
Next section: speaking one. This section covers speaking patterns for explaining historical events: definitions, time, quantity, results, and causes.
A grammar pattern used to define something, meaning that a term refers to or means a certain thing. It is useful when explaining a concept.
Use it for the first sentence of an explanation, like in a history presentation.
Division means that a country is split.
A grammar pattern meaning that one thing is the short form of another. It is how you explain abbreviations.
It is handy for explaining acronyms, like the names of organisations.
The UN is short for the United Nations.
A suffix meaning for a certain period of time. It attaches directly to a time expression.
It stresses how long something lasted, and you will see it a lot in news and writing.
I lived in Korea for three years.
An expression for the early, middle, or late part of a decade. It is attached after a decade like the eighties.
Early can be shortened to one syllable, and late can be replaced by a short word meaning the end.
팔십 년대 초반에 민주화 운동이 커졌어요.
The democracy movement grew in the early eighties.
An expression meaning at that time. It refers back to a period that has been mentioned already.
It is more formal than the everyday phrase for back then, and fits history writing.
At that time, Korea was a poor country.
An expression meaning after a period of time, with the feeling of finally. It follows a time period.
It often means for the first time in a long while, as in meeting again after many years.
I went back to my hometown after ten years.
A pair of words meaning before and after. They are used with a point in time.
They are neutral time markers, great for timelines in history and news.
Before and after the war are very different.
A pair of words meaning right before and right after. They are stronger and closer than the plain pair.
Use them for the moment around an event, like right before an exam or right after a speech.
I get nervous right before the exam.
A prefix meaning several, giving a rough but large count. It attaches to numbers like tens and hundreds.
Put it before ten, hundred, or thousand to say dozens, hundreds, or thousands.
Hundreds of people gathered in the square.
A suffix meaning and some, or about. It follows a number to say the amount is slightly more than that.
It is a written style way to give approximate numbers.
About two hundred people took part.
A pair of words expressing surprise about a quantity. One means as many as, the other means only.
Choose between them to show whether the number is surprisingly big or surprisingly small.
As many as ten thousand people gathered.
A pair of words meaning at least and at most. They set the lower and upper limits.
They give you a range, which is helpful in plans, budgets, and statistics.
It takes at least an hour.
A grammar pattern meaning to end up doing something or to come to a situation. It shows a result that was not simply planned by the speaker.
It is very useful for describing how circumstances changed, like how you came to live somewhere.
I ended up working in Korea.
A grammar pattern meaning due to or because of. It attaches to a noun and gives the cause of an event.
It sounds formal and is common in news, especially for bad events.
전쟁으로 인해서 많은 사람이 고향을 떠났어요.
Because of the war, many people left their hometowns.
That was every word of chapter eight. Play it again tomorrow, and try to say each Korean word before you hear it.
